messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm out of memory error
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet users,

I am trying to estimate an ERGM and keep getting an error that not
enough memory can be allocated.  The code I'm using and the
corresponding error message are included below.  

I'm trying to recreate and modify the analyses from Goodreau et al's
statnet tutorial in the Journal of Statistical Software.  I'm using the
faux.mesa.high data, which has 205 vertices and 203 edges.  The problem
appears when I add the gwdegree parameter to a model that otherwise
includes only nodematch terms.  I've increased the memory available to R
but that does not help.  Based on what I've read in previous posts, it
doesn't appear that the network is too large or that there are too many
rows or terms in the model.  I'm using version 2.1 of statnet and
version 2.8 of R.  

I would appreciate any suggestions to overcome this error.

Thanks,
David

> memory.limit(4000)
> fmh <- faux.mesa.high
> model4b <- ergm(fmh ~ edges + nodematch("Grade") + nodematch("Race") +

  nodematch("Sex") + gwdegree(1, fixed=FALSE), MCMCsamplesize = 1e+5,
maxit

  seed = 123)

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm out of memory error
messages.body_plain:
Hi David.  I'm not sure why you're getting an error about trying to  
allocate an object of 158.7 Mb, which doesn't seem that large to me,  
but nonetheless one suggestion I have is to use "fixed=TRUE" (perhaps  
with several values of the parameter) as in Section 7 of the JSS  
article you mention instead of "fixed=FALSE".  It is MUCH more  
computationally intensive to do "fixed=FALSE" because the ergm routine  
is trying to fit a complicated curved exponential family model,  
whereas with "fixed=TRUE" the model is actually just a standard ergm.

Hope this helps,
Dave

David Hunter
Associate professor
Department of Statistics
Penn State University
Phone:  (814) 863-0979
Fax:  (814) 863-7114
www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] questions about statnet
messages.body_plain:
Hi Elena,

I can't help you with the first question, but I can tell you how I 
solved the second.

Say you have a graph called "net" and two vectors (the length of which 
corresponds to the number of vertices in your graph): "gpa" and "race". 
  Set these as vertex attributes:

set.vertex.attribute(net,"gpa",floor(gpa)+2) # gpa=1 => triangle
set.vertex.attribute(net,"race", race)

Now you can plot the graph:

plot(net,
      vertex.col="race",
      vertex.sides="gpa"
      edge.lwd=1)

You can do more tweaking, but that's the general idea.  You can rig your 
colors to be something more mnemonic using palette().  Type this command 
at the R prompt and you will see what the default color order is. Either 
set the race such that they correspond to the colors you want or change 
the order in palette() -- just remember what you did to change it!

Hope this helps.

Cheers,

Jamie

messages.subject: [statnet_help] longitudinal analyses
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,

Sorry it has taken so long to respond to your email.  The short answer is 
that the development team is hard at work developing a fully dynamic 
modeling capacity in statnet.  Some of this is functional now in our 
development code, and the rest is likely to be within the next 6-9 months.

There are two types of dynamics in networks: dynamics that govern ties 
(formation, dissolution, attribute changes) and dynamics that govern nodes 
(entry, exit, attribute changes).  We've been calling these "tie dynamics" 
and "vital dynamics" respectively.

We have a working version of a simple tie dynamic process up and running 
now in our development version of statnet.  It uses an ERGM model to 
govern tie formation, and one or more duration parameters to govern tie 
dissolution.  The size and composition of the network are fixed.  We have 
used this model to simulate an epidemic over a network where the ties form 
and dissolve over time, preserving a set of mean statistics (defined by 
the ERGM terms) and a duration distribution (both estimated from data). 
A paper that uses this model this will be published in the American 
Journal of Public Health in June 2009.

One of our graduate students, Pavel Krivitsky, is currently working on 
developing the modeling framework for vital dynamics in his dissertation. 
The fundamental question for the model is: what stays invariant as network 
size and composition change?  The answer depends in part on what kind of 
data you have.  Even cross sectional network data can be used to drive a 
fully dynamic network simulation, if you are willing to make assumptions 
about the parts of the process that you do not observe.  Pavel is 
presenting a paper up at the NIPS conference (today!) that presents one 
approach to that topic.

Making the network fully dynamic (tie and vital) also requires reworking 
some of the data storage and retrieval aspects of the code.  We have been 
developing the specifications for that over the past month, and hope to 
have the framework settled by the end of January.

If you (or others) are interested in more discussion about this, let us 
know.  If there are specific kinds of functionality that you would like to 
see implemented, it's a good time to speak up.  We can't promise to make 
it happen in the first pass, but if it is easy to incorporate, we will.

best of the season to all,
Martina

> ever seen an error like this?

Hi Elena,

My first guess would be that you have an NA for at least one student's 
parental education level in your data.  Is that right?  I do believe that 
smalldiff as written does not handle missing attribute values.

If that's the problem, then you might consider somehow imputing your 
missing values. Better, more model-based approaches to handling missing 
data in ergms are in development, but I would consider starting there.

If that's not the problem, let me know and I'll brainstorm some more.

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] gof p-values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin.  The idea behind the MCMC p-value is simply that you  
calculate what proportion of the "null" distribution (in this case,  
represented by the 100 simulated values) is at least as extreme as the  
observed statistic.  Here, I believe that "at least as extreme" means  
"at least as far from the sample mean", which would give essentially a  
2-sided hypothesis test of the null that says the observed came from  
the same distribution as the simulations, though I'm not 100% sure  
that's the exact method of calculation.

You are therefore correct that large p-values in this instance are  
"good", in the sense that they give no evidence that the null  
hypothesis is false (i.e., no evidence that the observed stat comes  
from a different distribution than the simulated stats).

Hope this helps.

Dave
